12. What stays private

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-12-privacy.Rmd
book-12-privacy.Rmd

What you will learn

Distinguish a private assignment from an aggregate release, understand distinct-person support, and recognise refused identifiers and free text.

This chapter uses the synthetic questionnaire dataset described in Getting started.

You need: the packages and the matching practice connection described in Before you start. Run its sections in order. Each chapter starts from a fresh practice connection; all the outputs below come from real dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.5 calls. The numbers describe teaching data, not clinical findings.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the book-work directory created in Getting started. Run this setup first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/fixture.R")
practice <- book_fixture()
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

The site connection is ready. This chapter creates its temporary questionnaire dataset locally.

Know which side holds each object

On your computer On each server
Recipe definitions, concept sets and parameters Database records and credentials
Public table/column/vocabulary metadata Pseudonymous person and episode rows
Output symbol names Exact permitted dates, ages and derived columns
Disclosure-checked aggregates Intermediate populations and joins

A symbol is the name of a server object. Seeing the name does not give you its contents. Pseudonymisation replaces person IDs for protected processing; it does not make a patient-level table suitable for download.

private <- omop_recipe(variables = list(age = omop_age_at("2024-06-01")),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(private, out = c(people = "D_private"), conns = conns))
#>      people 
#> "D_private"

The mapping is the result you receive from recipe execution. Exact completed age stays beside the source data. This is called publication into the DataSHIELD session; it is not public publication on the internet or a row export.

YouChoose events, variables and outputs.
→
ServerCompute with private records and apply release checks.
→
You seeSymbol names, schemas and checked summaries.

Request an aggregate 

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_private$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 24
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>   5%  10%  25%  50%  75%  90%  95% Mean 
#>   34   34   34   43   49   49   49   42

An approved aggregate method checks its own disclosure rules. A successfully assigned table does not guarantee every later summary or model will be releasable. The book’s outputs are genuine results of those methods, not downloaded rows.

Note

A private assignment is not a row download. Every later aggregate uses the disclosure rules of its own method.

The final release rule

Each final patient component needs enough distinct persons for the server’s nfilter.subset. Many events from one person still contribute only one person to this check. The practice server uses the ordinary threshold of five. Thresholds are server policy, not something the analyst lowers to obtain a desired answer.

Intermediate calculations may contain small populations privately. The gate is at final publication; a joined result’s private inputs do not need separate published symbols. A standalone filter produces a final object and is gated. Here we intentionally request a subset with no qualifying rows:

small_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.filter("D_private", expr = omop_where(age > 200L),
    newobj = "D_too_small", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(small_message, "\n")
#> OMOP filter failed and was rolled back: site: Disclosive: operation blocked - insufficient individuals to meet disclosure threshold. No further details available.; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The refusal reports the policy boundary without providing the small private count. The previous D_private object remains available. Empty and undersized results share this protection; do not interpret the diagnostic as a patient count.

Why identifiers and source text are refused

Class 1 includes direct identifiers, source identifiers and free text that may contain identifiers. Renaming a source field does not make it safe. Both output values and predicates are checked, so a count cannot be used to probe a forbidden text column. The following intentionally invalid definition demonstrates that check:

text_message <- tryCatch({
  blocked <- omop_recipe(variables = list(answer = omop_variable(
    event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L, value = "value_as_string"),
    reducer = omop_reduce("first_value"))),
    outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
  recipe_to_plan(blocked)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(text_message, "\n")
#> Disclosive: the plan requests blocked (class-1) column(s) that the server can never release or filter on: value_as_string (event 'obs_900002' value).

This definition is refused before execution. Use the reviewed coded answer value_as_concept_id and translated categories when it answers the question, as in chapter 10. Free text is not needed for that analysis.

Why dates and ages can remain private columns

Class 2 means a quasi-identifier: a value that may help identify someone when combined with other facts. Exact dates, birth components and ages are permitted on these private assignment paths, without an owner-side date switch. Their aggregates and any category labels still face the applicable release controls.

date_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(visit_date = omop_date("first_visit")),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(date_recipe, out = c(people = "D_private_date"), conns = conns))
#>           people 
#> "D_private_date"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_private_date", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"  "visit_date"

You see the schema, not the dates. Turning an exact date into a factor publishes category labels as metadata, which needs its own support checks. A fine custom date pattern can therefore be refused even when a private Date column is permitted. Coarsen to the scientifically appropriate month/quarter/year and request an approved aggregate; do not encode a disallowed field into another name or type.

Protected keys cannot become analyst variables 

key_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.mutate("D_private", copied = person_id,
    newobj = "D_key_copy", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(key_message, "\n")
#> OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: column 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be used in an expression; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The server needs keys to align rows and joins; an analyst mutation cannot copy, rewrite or filter them. Use the declared population and join operations instead.

Recipe protection is not a DP promise

The recipes, table assignments and dsBase analyses in this book use ordinary DataSHIELD disclosure controls. They do not acquire a differential-privacy (DP) guarantee just because dsOMOP also provides protected OHDSI release routes. Those routes have separate contracts and provenance; inspect them when using those services. Deterministic noise is not a reason to repeat a request until an answer changes. There are no per-analyst call budgets or history-dependent answers in this design.

No chapter needs raw-row download methods, weaker thresholds, database TLS changes or owner configuration to make its normal protected recipe route work.

Try it

After the refused small filter, confirm you can still summarise the original private age column.

Solution

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_private$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 24
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>   5%  10%  25%  50%  75%  90%  95% Mean 
#>   34   34   34   43   49   49   49   42

The original object remains usable. A refusal is not permission to bypass its release rule with another encoding.

Exercise 2: a common variant

Confirm a failed key-copy attempt left the original schema usable.

Solution 2

dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_private", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id" "age"

The protected key was not turned into an analyst variable; the original private object remains.

Exercise 3: a pitfall to avoid

Check a valid date recipe is still a local definition. Does serialisation release dates?

Solution 3

is.character(recipe_export_json(date_recipe))
#> [1] TRUE

No. A JSON definition is public study logic. The resulting dates remain private and aggregates still face release checks.

Recap

A recipe creates private objects and returns their names. Final patient outputs need distinct-person support; aggregates and category metadata have further checks. Class-1 fields and protected-key expressions are refused.
